preamble: Devoicing of the voiced dental fricative [ð] to [θ] occurs in final position and next to voiceless consonants. Gothic devoiced post-vocalic [ð] (the fricative allophone of /d/) at the end of a word, spelling it ⟨þ⟩ and producing alternations such as biuþs 'table' beside genitive biudis. Icelandic devoices /ð/ before a pause and, in Southern accents, before aspirated stops. In north-central Peninsular Spanish, word-final /d/, otherwise [ð], is variably realized as voiceless [θ], as in ciudad [θi̯uˈðaθ] and colloquial Madrid [maˈðɾiθ].

examples.note: Post-vocalic /d/ was the fricative [ð] before voiced sounds and was devoiced to [θ], spelled ⟨þ⟩, at the end of a word or before /s/; the plural biudōs keeps ⟨d⟩.
Same alternation in the adjective, from Proto-Germanic *bauþaz, *baudaz.
Voiced consonants are devoiced word-finally before a pause; the medial /ð/ stays voiced.
In Southern accents /ð/ is devoiced next to a following aspirated stop.

languageExamples.context: Before a pause, and before aspirated stops in Southern accents

examples.note: Word-final /d/, realized as [ð] in most varieties, becomes voiceless [θ] in parts of Spain; Hualde and Eager (2016) found voiceless fricatives in all phrasal contexts in conversational Castilian, more often before a pause than before a vowel.
The colloquial pronunciation of the city's name in the Madrid area.

sources: Bedinghaus, R., & Sedó, B. (2014). Intervocalic /d/ deletion in Málaga: Frequency effects and linguistic factors. IULC Working Papers 14. https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/iulcwp/article/view/26207
